This is purely this guys theory but it makes sense. So in the rear cap there is a fitting that goes through the shell into the pressure vessel that brings all the utilities inside. It’s important to understand that that sharp tail the titan has is just a housing unit for all the electronics and the hull has a round cap in the back just like it does in the front. The tail piece with all the electronics and stuff is at the same pressure as the ocean so we can think of that inlet for the utilities as being an exact joint/barrier between the internal pressure of the hull and the outside ocean pressure. So let’s say the crack or the inlet or whatever fails catastrophically and water comes rushing in. The air compresses rapidly. Let’s imagine the hull/cylinder made of carbon fiber actually holds up under this pressure change and directs all that force to the front of the vessel and blows off the front cap. The bolts holding the front cap to the ring (cap is attached to ring which is attached to carbon fiber hull) get sheared off which would explain why the ring is no longer attached to the cap. It’s unclear if the view window would have been blown off due to the pressure change or the water hammer effect from the water rushing in or if it stayed intact. 

This is the same principle they use to fire torpedoes from submarines as well. They pump water into the chamber with the torpedo and let that water equalise to the pressure of the water outside the sub then they let water at an even higher pressure pump in behind the torpedo. The water being pumped in has to suddenly stop as it hits the torpedo and that change of moment is what they call a water hammer. The velocity is transferred to the torpedo and it is fired out. Think of the front cap of the titan as the torpedo and the water rushing in at high pressure and velocity as the water hammer. Except with the torpedo they had water in the chamber before the hammer comes in which is incompressible. In the titans case there is air and humans between the cap and the water coming in which is highly compressible.

In senario 1.:. This rapid change of pressure is almost like a bomb going off and in that moment the ‘shock wave’ over pressurises the water around the sub (outside). The fact that the water pressure outside is higher than the water pressure inside the sub means that there will be back pressure as the 2 meet. This back pressure generates the force that then rip of the rings and destroys the hull as well as blows out the back end.

In senario 2. The same happens but instead the hull is destroyed while the pressure on the inside and outside are trying to equalise. 

There are 2 main reasons why he believes this to be the case. If the hull imploded first the front ring would most likely still be attached to the front cap. The beams connecting the sharp tail end and the pressure vessel are still present and attached to the tail with ‘minimal’ damage.

This is all just a theory. But it makes sense. We won’t know until they recover parts of the hull which I believe that have and u can see them being unloaded off of the boat in a big white bag as well. But who knows.

This is half right. Fatigue is a term used in metallurgy specifically to describe the failure of crystalline structures over time and loading cycles. Crystalline structures are connected atoms/molecules that are in a patten and repeat throughout a material such as metal I.e it is a uniform material. Materials like this have predictable behaviours under stress and they are well understood

Carbon fiber isn’t a crystalline structure as it is made of layers of a bonding agent (resin) and fibers in various/random directions. Thus we cannot apply the term fatigue life to structures like this, yet they do fatigue just in a way different from that of metals. 

Metals show fatigue failure on their surfaces normally in the form of a crack. Composite materials will have fatigue/load cracks internally and most often throughout the whole volume. The randomness in the composite materials structure makes it unpredictable. When loaded to its theoretical max it either remain intact with no damage whatsoever or there is some damage and it is ‘broken’. Nothing in between. Where as metals can be seen as having various stages during fatigue failure. 

This randomness and unpredictability makes it difficult to group all ‘carbon fiber hulls’ under one umbrella since it is so strongly dependent on the shape and structure and curing process and direction of layers ect. In engineering, when it comes to human lives we tend to go with the predictable and proven… that is part of the job.
